p.src: 1. The tradition of historical narrative began with Master Zuo, yet critics still fault him for departing from the truth; how much more must this be true of popular tales! Yet when the intent is chiefly to encourage virtue and punish vice, even invention is no offense. The fiction writers of our age have produced works of every kind, many of which forsake the Classics and rebel against the Way, and cannot serve as instruction. Now and then, a writer borrows a theme to expound a lesson, seeking to warn and awaken readers by depicting murder, theft, lust, and falsehood; but some are mere patchworks rather than complete books, while others fabricate embellishments unlike anything ordinarily known; though they catch the eyes of those enamored of novelty, in truth they only deepen the decline of refined tradition. How can they compare with the rectitude of this book? Former worthies compared it to the writings of Ban Gu and Sima Qian; I would say it advances even beyond Zuo Qiuming and almost preserves the lingering intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals. It therefore fully deserves to be called a “tradition.”

p.src: 1. Liangshan Marsh lies within Yanzhou Prefecture in Shandong. The local gazetteer writes the name with the character luo and calls it eight hundred li across—an exaggeration. Yet men of old wished to drain this marsh and found it difficult to contain its waters, so it cannot have been small. The tale names neither Liangshan nor Song Jiang in its title, for the place was not inherently a bandits’ lair, nor was the man inherently a bandit; hence it is called merely Water Margin. Hu means the water’s edge: the wording deliberately leaves the place unspecified. This makes clear that all beneath Heaven are the sovereign’s subjects, and that Song Jiang never dared claim this marsh as his own. Might it express the longing of those dwelling by the sea? How subtle was Luo’s choice of title!

p.src: 1. Loyalty and righteousness are the virtues by which one serves one’s lord and treats one’s friends. A man without loyalty or righteousness is rotten even while alive, and however fine his words may be, they will not endure. These one hundred and eight men are loyalty and righteousness gathered among the wooded hills; these one hundred and twenty chapters are loyalty and righteousness made manifest in ink and brush. What is missing from the official histories must be sought in the records of unofficial chroniclers; what is missing among the robed and capped must be sought among the common folk. The aim was to stir men of virtue while denying petty men any excuse to pursue their selfish ends. There was thus good reason for Master Li to restore the two words “Loyalty and Righteousness” to the title.

p.src: 1. A book benefits from critical annotations, for they can reveal the author’s intent and open the reader’s mind. When done well, they are like adding fur to bring a creature to life and dotting the pupils of its eyes, fully revealing its spirit and brilliance; when done poorly, they are like slapping cheeks and smearing a face, defiling the original. This is not a task to be undertaken carelessly. In this edition, the purpose of the whole work, the telling admonition of each chapter, and the spirit of every phrase and character have all been brought to light, so that readers may know this is a popular chronicle written with a historian’s brush, one that bears upon the moral order of the age and benefits literary composition, utterly unlike the commercial editions of the past. Like performing from a musical score and striking every beat, or needling a bronze acupuncture figure and finding every point, the annotator’s brush possesses tongue and eyes, enabling readers both to see and to hear. This is what is most precious in critical annotation.

p.src: 1. This book exhaustively depicts human feelings and circumstances and is already a portrait drawn from life; would adding illustrations not be nearly superfluous? Even so, how many people can perceive King Wen in the zither or behold Yao in a wall? The portraits on Cloud Terrace and in Lingyan Pavilion, and the illustrations of “The Seventh Month” and “The Wandering People,” can stir, inspire, grieve, and move viewers, making the subjects seem present before them. Images therefore cannot be dispensed with. Here we have devised a new approach rather than following old models: some images stand separately outside the chapter headings, while others are interspersed within the chapters. Only the finest scenes have been selected, for abundance is not what matters.

p.src: 1. Ancient editions contained a prefatory address by Luo and transmitted such episodes as that of “Granny Lampwick,” but these can no longer be seen; later editors, constrained by the scheme of the Four Great Outlaws, cut the work to fit it, while others, finding one hundred and twenty chapters too cumbersome, pruned it down. Both approaches were mistaken. The edition of Guo Wuding is the old text; its relocation of the episode concerning Yan Po is highly judicious. Yet in its treatment of the outlaws, removing Wang Qing and Tian Hu while adding the Liao kingdom remains merely a lesser writer’s method of making the parts correspond. They fail to understand that a master writer does not proceed in this way. In the present work, for example, Wang Jin opens the narrative but is never brought back to close his thread. Is this not precisely what distinguishes it from all other novels and makes it the sage among novels?

p.src: 1. The old edition removed the clutter of poems and songs, partly from concern that they would interrupt the course of events and partly lest they distract the reader’s eye; the result was admirably direct and lucid. Yet some verses serve to portray human bearing or shape the rises and falls of literary feeling, and these cannot all be discarded. We have therefore augmented and revised them anew: in some places altering the original text to advance what it already contained, and in others retracing the intentions of the ancients to add what it lacked. The sole purpose is to encourage virtue and punish vice while also making good use of humor, so that readers may be moved at heart, break into smiles, and find no lack of lingering matter for admiration and reflection.

p.src: 1. The old edition also devoted considerable effort to correcting the text, pronunciations, and characters, yet many confusions, errors, inconsistencies, and corruptions remained. The lyric quoted at the very beginning, for example, contains no fewer than four errors. A collation of this edition against the old one will reveal the rest. Cases such as writing “耐” for “奈,” or “躁” for “燥,” may still be called simple scribal errors. But confusing “戴” with “帶,” “煞” with “殺,” or “閂” with “拴”; failing to distinguish “ ” from “衝,” or “逕” from “竟,” causes the meaning itself to go astray. Examples of this kind are too numerous to enumerate; all have now been collated and corrected. Placing pronunciations directly beneath the characters does make them easy to see; but their varying sizes and broken continuity offend learned readers. We have therefore gathered them all at the end of each chapter for convenient reference. If the earlier occurrence is far removed, a representative example is given; if the pronunciation differs, it is listed separately. Where even part of the character remains legible or the colloquial meaning is intelligible, it has sometimes been omitted.

p.src: 1. Those who set words before the world must have some basis for them. This book, however, creates events from the truth of human feeling and originally had no need to seek corroboration in other works. Moreover, the names and number of persons recorded in the Mirror of the Song and the Anecdotes of the Xuanhe Era can indeed be verified; the Classified Drafts from the Seven Revisions also records their names, stating that Guanzhong wrote of the Thirty-six Heavenly Spirits and the Seventy-two Earthly Fiends. We have now placed these two texts at the head of the volume and also listed the native places and origins of all one hundred and eight men, making them convenient to consult and remember and furnishing material for conversation.

p.src: 1. A recorder of events extracts their essentials, while a compiler of sayings draws out their hidden import. In this tale, the episodes of Li Kui have already been extracted to form a separate Life of the Magistrate of Shouzhang. Lu Da, , Wu Song, Shi Xiu, Zhang Shun, Li Jun, Yan Qing, and others could likewise each be made the subject of a separate biography showing the whole course of his life. As for its excellent and memorable phrases, even its dialect expressions, jokes, and curses are enough to stir the human heart. We have therefore singled them out here to show that this book is filled with scattered gold, more than one could ever finish gathering. Master Su Dongpo said, “The proper way to read a book is to seek one particular meaning from it each time.” If even a novel possesses beauties such as these, how much more must the official histories!
